THE VIRTUAL PHYSIOLOGY LABORATORY

Lung and chest wall statics

Change the compliance of the lung or the chest wall and watch the compliance curves, FRC, TLC, and RV move. The lungs want to be small, the chest wall wants to be big, and FRC is where the two pulls balance.

Sets how far muscles can push the system toward TLC and RV

The lung compliance multiplier changes the slope of the lung curve and, more modestly, the lung's size: an emphysematous lung is bigger at every pressure and a fibrotic lung smaller. The chest wall compliance multiplier divides the chest wall's recoil, pivoting near RV, so a stiffer chest wall also has a smaller resting volume.

THINK THROUGH THE RESPONSE

Where do the pulls balance?

At FRC the lung recoils inward and the chest wall recoils outward with equal and opposite pressures. Which way should FRC move if the lung becomes stiffer?

Lung volumes

Mechanics at FRC

Compliance (pressure–volume) curves

Hover over the plot or use the slider to add the lung and chest wall pressures at any volume

● Lung● Chest wall● Lung + chest wall┅ Muscles

The muscles lower pleural pressure. Follow the chain: Ppl falls, PA drops below atmospheric, air flows in, the lung fills, and its recoil rises until PA is back to zero. Then the muscles relax and the recoil pushes the air back out. Try it again in fibrosis.

HOW THE CURVES COMBINE

Same volume, pressures add

The lung and chest wall are coupled by the pleural space, so they always have the same volume (except in pneumothorax). To hold the relaxed system at any volume, you need the pressure that holds the lung there plus the pressure that holds the chest wall there:

Prs(V) = Ptp(V) + Ppl(V)

With no airflow and the muscles relaxed, these are the lecture's pressures. The lung's elastic recoil, Pel, equals the transpulmonary pressure, Ptp = PA − Ppl. The chest wall's recoil is the pleural pressure, Ppl, about −5 cmH₂O at FRC. Their sum is the alveolar pressure, PA, which is zero at FRC.

So the combined curve is built by adding the two curves horizontally, along the pressure axis, at each volume. Take the slope of both sides:

1 / Crs = 1 / CL + 1 / Ccw

That is the rule for compliances in series, like two springs hooked end to end. The combined system is always stiffer than either part. Compare the vascular compliances in the circulation, which sit side by side at the same pressure and add directly (Ctotal = C1 + C2). Adding the lung and chest wall volumes at the same pressure would be the parallel rule, and it gives the wrong curve.

The chest wall rests at about 72% of vital capacity (Rahn et al., 1946). Below that volume it springs outward and helps you inhale. Above it, the chest wall recoils inward too, so both structures resist further inflation. That is why the combined curve flattens and compliance falls as you approach TLC.

What sets FRC, TLC, and RV. FRC takes no muscle effort. It is the volume where the lung’s inward recoil and the chest wall’s outward recoil cancel, so the respiratory system curve (lung + chest wall) crosses zero. TLC and RV are where the muscles reach their limit against that recoil. The red dashed muscle curves show the most pressure the muscles can make at each volume. Near TLC the lung is close to its full size, so its curve turns almost flat. Even a much stronger push would add little volume, and the lung’s elastic properties set most of TLC. Three things set RV: the lung’s elastic recoil, how far the chest wall can be compressed, and, in nonsmokers under about 40, expiratory muscle effort. This model shows the young adult: the expiratory muscles reach their limit against a chest wall that resists further compression. With age, smoking, or airway disease, the lung loses recoil, small airways close first, and RV is higher. Weaken the muscles and both muscle curves move in: TLC falls, RV rises, and FRC stays put. A stiff lung lowers TLC for a different reason: its curve meets the muscle curve at a lower volume, where the inspiratory muscles are longer and can push harder.

Pressure times volume is work. During a breath the muscles do elastic work equal to the area under the combined curve between FRC and the end of inspiration (shaded during the breath). A stiffer lung or chest wall makes the curve steeper, so the same tidal volume takes a larger pleural pressure swing and more work.

Model details. Lung: V = Vmax − (Vmax − V0)·e−kP (Salazar–Knowles exponential), with a minimal volume (“minimal air”) V0 of 1.25 L, below RV, and Vmax 6.27 L. A lung compliance multiplier s scales the slope by s and both volumes by s0.25, so TLC can rise above 120% of predicted in emphysema and RV can fall in fibrosis. Chest wall: logistic curve resting at 4.75 L (72% VC), −5 cmH₂O at FRC and −14 cmH₂O at RV; compliance changes pivot it at 1.5 L. Compliance is read as the slope at FRC, so it can differ from the slider multiplier when FRC moves along a curved line. Healthy values: FRC 3.0 L, TLC 6.0 L, RV 1.5 L, CL 0.28, Ccw 0.29, Crs 0.14 L/cmH₂O. Muscle limits: the most pressure the muscles can add, on the same axis as the relaxation curves (Rahn et al., 1946). The most pressure the inspiratory muscles can make falls 13 cmH₂O for each liter of lung volume toward TLC, and the expiratory muscles’ maximum falls 33 cmH₂O per liter toward RV, which puts maximal mouth pressures near −110 cmH₂O at RV and +200 cmH₂O at TLC, close to normal adult values (Black and Hyatt, 1969). The strength slider scales both. TLC and RV are where the combined curve meets these limits. RV here is where the expiratory muscles can no longer compress the stiffening chest wall, as in young adults. Airway closure, which raises RV with age and in emphysema, is modeled on the PFT page. Breath: Ppl = Pcw(V) − Pmus, PA = Ppl + Pel(V), flow = −PA/Raw with Raw 3 cmH₂O·s/L. Pmus is set so every condition reaches the same 0.5 L tidal volume; work = ∫Prs dV (1 cmH₂O·L = 0.098 J).
